events.title: The Berlin Wall opens
events.description: East Germans begin crossing the border freely. The change becomes a powerful symbol of a changing Europe.

events.title: Hubble launches into orbit
events.description: The space telescope leaves Earth aboard Discovery. Its first images later reveal a flaw in the main mirror.

events.title: The Soviet Union breaks apart
events.description: Gorbachev resigns as Soviet president. Independent states take the place of the union.

events.title: Web software becomes free to use
events.description: CERN releases its World Wide Web software into the public domain, helping others build on it.

what_happened_next.text:
The US share basket almost doubled and led these seven choices. Boeing gained too, but IBM lost about two-fifths of its value. Sony and the international basket rose only modestly. A large aircraft order book and a familiar electronics brand did not remove the uncertainty of owning their shares.

The years ahead brought major political change. The Berlin Wall opened in November 1989, and the Soviet Union broke apart in December 1991. Hubble launched into orbit in 1990. In 1993, CERN made its World Wide Web software free for others to use and build on.

Those events help explain what the world was like, but they are not a formula for the return of each stock. The investments followed different paths through the same history.

Here, owning a wide mix of US companies worked better than choosing any one of the three featured businesses. That is a result for this period, not a promise for the next one. Compare the losses and gains along the route as well as the final amounts.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: Airlines were ordering new jets, music buyers were changing formats, and major diplomatic talks were beginning.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: Different businesses and markets delivered different results. Owning many companies helped avoid depending entirely on a struggling company such as IBM.
reflection.what_faded_away: Predictions that vinyl records were finished did not predict the returns of an electronics company or a whole stock market.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: The end of the Cold War and the precise company rankings were unknown. Strong demand in one industry was not a guarantee for every related investment.

hot_stock_outcomes.text: Boeing’s 1990 profit rose 42% to about $1.4 billion. The business later slowed: in November 1992, weaker orders led it to announce lower 757 and 767 production. The investment still ended higher. Strong early earnings and later airline cutbacks both belong in the story of these five years.

IBM lost nearly $5 billion in 1992, including heavy costs to reorganize the company. Lou Gerstner became chief executive in April 1993, and more job cuts followed that year. The investment finished well below its starting value. A leadership change offered a new direction, but the turnaround was still unfinished at this endpoint.

Sony bought Columbia Pictures in November 1989, adding movies to its electronics and music businesses. Its film group went on to lead the North American box office for three years through 1993. Even with hit films, the investment gained only a little over this window: success in one division did not promise a large return for the whole company.
